extracted.intended_audience: educators, curriculum designers, teachers, and educational reformers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for selecting, organizing, and using subject-matter and activities in school so they promote democratic ideals, social insight, and integrated intellectual growth rather than rote mechanical training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject matter supplies meanings for social life
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject matter of education consists primarily of the meanings which supply content to existing social life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select, formulate, and organize subject matter so it transmits the meanings of present collective experience to the new generation rather than treating subject matter as valuable in itself separate from its function in promoting meanings in the learner's present experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present problems relevant to living together
rubrics_metrics.description: A curriculum which acknowledges the social responsibilities of education must present situations where problems are relevant to the problems of living together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design observation and information tasks calculated to develop social insight and interest; avoid material divorced from everyday social relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin from learners' experience and capacities
rubrics_metrics.description: The desirability of starting from and with the experience and capacities of learners has led to introduction of forms of activity, in play and work, similar to activities children engage in outside school.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use learners' existing impulses and experiences as the basis for instruction rather than imposing abstract, ready-made content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include play and active work as regular program elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Play and active work should be part of the regular school program for intellectual and social reasons, not merely as agreeable diversions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When exercises prompted by native tendencies (explore, manipulate tools, construct, express emotion) are regular, the whole pupil is engaged, school-life gap is reduced, and cooperative social learning arises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage the whole pupil
rubrics_metrics.description: Active occupations engage the whole pupil, reducing the artificial gap between life in school and out and affording motives for attention to a wide variety of educative materials and processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor activities that combine intellectual and social engagement rather than isolated drills that train only a narrow faculty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid activities that are mere prescription or duplication
rubrics_metrics.description: Activities which follow definite prescription and dictation or reproduce without modification ready-made models may give muscular dexterity but do not require perception and elaboration of ends nor permit use of judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject rote, tightly prescribed exercises (including many traditional kindergarten and manual training practices) that prevent initiative and judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide opportunity for mistakes and constructive failure
rubrics_metrics.description: Opportunity for making mistakes is an incidental requirement because forbidding mistakes restricts initiative, reduces judgment, and compels use of methods remote from life's complex situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose materials and tasks that allow however-limited chances for error and consequence so learners learn limits of capacity and are stimulated to improve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize creative constructive attitude over external finish
rubrics_metrics.description: It is more important to keep alive a creative and constructive attitude than to secure an external perfection by engaging the pupil's action in too minute and too closely regulated pieces of work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insist on accuracy and finish only in parts of a complex work within the pupil's capacity; avoid overemphasis on finish at expense of initiative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use crude/raw materials rather than over-formed materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Starting with crude material and subjecting it to purposeful handling is necessary for the pupil to gain the intelligence embodied in finished material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid supplying only perfected, shaped materials that prevent errors and simulate intelligence; provide raw materials that require selection, adaptation, and judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus active occupations on wholes (functional situations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Active occupations should be concerned primarily with wholes: the functional development of a situation (a qualitative completeness of appeal) rather than isolated physical elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize tasks around purposive activities whose unity gives single meaning to constituent elements rather than presenting parts as 'simple' isolated things for beginners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose occupations that typify social situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Active occupations may typify social situations because men's fundamental common concerns center about food, shelter, clothing, household furnishings, and appliances connected with production, exchange, and consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select activities (gardening, weaving, cooking, woodworking, etc.) that reflect real social functions so knowledge and skill are transferable and socially meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat occupations as intrinsically valuable and liberalizing
rubrics_metrics.description: In schools, occupations are not carried on for pecuniary gain but for their own content; freed from wage-earning they supply modes of experience which are intrinsically valuable and truly liberalizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame manual and domestic activities as educational ends in themselves, revealing scientific content and social value rather than merely vocational preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use occupations as opportunities for scientific study
rubrics_metrics.description: Activities like gardening afford avenues of approach to knowledge (botany, chemistry, physics) and can introduce scientific facts and principles connected with the activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate subject-matter (e.g., plant growth, soil chemistry) into purposeful occupations so students move naturally from activity-based interest to deliberate intellectual investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use occupations to teach social sciences concretely
rubrics_metrics.description: The most direct road for elementary students into civics and economics is found in consideration of the place and office of industrial occupations in social life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach civics and economics less as abstract bodies of formulated knowledge and more through direct subject-matter found in students' daily social groups and occupations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active occupations introduce the experimental method
rubrics_metrics.description: Active occupations in which appliances are brought to bear upon physical things with intention of effecting useful changes are the most vital introduction to the experimental method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design hands-on occupations that require controlling conditions, observing outcomes, and testing—connecting everyday making to scientific experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize play and work as purpose-driven activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Both play and industry involve ends consciously entertained and the selection and adaptations of materials and processes designed to effect the desired ends; their difference is largely one of time-span.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design activities so play retains directing ideas and foresight rather than being mere aimless motion; allow play to be free and plastic while linking it to purposeful adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure play includes anticipatory forecasting and direction
rubrics_metrics.description: Play has an end in the sense of a directing idea which gives point to successive acts; persons who play are trying to do or effect something and involve anticipatory forecasts which stimulate present responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid play activities that are purely physical, imitative, or hypnotic; encourage imaginative but directed play that fosters planning and adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide observable results to give sense of powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Observable results are necessary to enable persons to get a sense and a measure of their own powers; as activities become more complicated they gain meaning and pass into work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure tasks so learners can see tangible outcomes of effort; this sustains attention and enables maturation from play to sustained purposeful work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid economic coercion and reproduce non-coercive occupations
rubrics_metrics.description: Under unfree economic conditions work becomes drudgery; schools should reproduce industrial situations under conditions where occupation can be carried on for its own sake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure school occupations are free from external coercive pressures (wage-earning imperatives) so that activity remains intrinsically motivating rather than merely a means to external rewards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide for wholesome recreation and art in education
rubrics_metrics.description: Education must make adequate provision for enjoyment of recreative leisure and train capacity for seeking and finding it; art is again the answer to this demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include opportunities for reinvigoration and imaginative engagement to prevent perverse or illicit outlets for suppressed instincts and to foster lasting habits of mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use geography and history to extend meaning of activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Geography and history supply subject matter which gives background and outlook, intellectual perspective, to what might otherwise be narrow personal actions or mere forms of technical skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach geography/history not as remote, ready-made statements but integrated with activities so ordinary experience is enlarged in time and space connections and gains enduring substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mere amassing of disconnected information
rubrics_metrics.description: If geography and history are taught as ready-made studies learned simply because one is sent to school, a large number of statements remote from everyday experience are learned and mind becomes wooden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make information 'informing' by connecting it to active pursuits and direct interests; encourage curiosity that follows from meaningful activity rather than rote memorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render connections perceptible through conditions of performance
rubrics_metrics.description: The task of education is to see to it that activities are performed in such ways and under such conditions as render their consequences and connections as perceptible as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design learning environments where spatial, natural, and historical connections of ordinary acts are made evident—'learning geography' means perceiving spatial connections; 'learning history' means recognizing human connections.
